places.name: Roma
places.foundedNote: traditional (Varronian) foundation 21 April 753 BC; Republic from 509 BC

status.t: seat of the Senate under Odoacer and the Ostrogoths

places.summary: The city of the seven hills, perhaps a million inhabitants under Augustus, fed by eleven aqueducts by 226. Enclosed by the Servian wall (378 BC) and the Aurelian wall (271-275), sacked by the Gauls (390/387 BC), Alaric (410), Gaiseric (455) and Totila (546), and reduced to perhaps 30,000 people by the late 6th century.

places.name: Ostia
places.foundedNote: castrum of the later 4th century BC; tradition credits Ancus Marcius

status.t: seat of a quaestor for the grain supply

places.summary: Rome's harbour town at the old Tiber mouth, from a 2-hectare castrum to a city of perhaps 50,000 with multi-storey insulae, horrea and the Piazzale delle Corporazioni, where shipping guilds from Carthage to Narbo kept offices. It declined from the 3rd century as Portus took the trade.

places.name: Portus
places.foundedNote: Claudian harbour begun 42/46, inaugurated by Nero 64; Trajan's hexagonal basin c. 112
places.summary: Rome's artificial harbour north of Ostia: Claudius's outer basin, whose lighthouse stood on the sunk hulk of Caligula's obelisk ship, and Trajan's 32-hectare hexagon. Its loss to Vitiges in 537 cut Belisarius's supply in the siege of Rome.

places.name: Antium
places.summary: Volscian port whose captured ships' beaks (rostra) decorated the speakers' platform in the Forum after 338 BC. Later a resort with imperial villas; birthplace of Caligula and Nero.

places.name: Tusculum

status.t: first community incorporated with full citizenship (municipium)

places.summary: Latin hill town that received Roman citizenship in 381 BC, the prototype of the municipium. Home of Cato the Elder and of the Mamilii; Cicero's Tusculan villa gave its name to the Tusculan Disputations.

places.name: Praeneste

status.t: colonia Sullana after the massacre of its men

places.summary: Latin city with the vast terraced sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, whose oracle used lots (sortes). Marius the Younger held it against Sulla in 82 BC; on its fall Sulla executed the male population and planted a colony.

places.name: Tibur
places.summary: Latin city above the falls of the Anio, source of travertine for Roman building. Hadrian built his 120-hectare villa below it (c. 118-138), and Zenobia ended her days nearby.

places.name: Lavinium

status.t: ally with special treaty renewed annually

places.summary: Latin cult centre where Roman magistrates sacrificed to the Penates and Vesta on taking office. Excavations found the Thirteen Altars and a 7th-century BC tumulus rebuilt in the 4th century as a heroon of Aeneas.

places.name: Aricia
places.summary: Latin town on the Via Appia beside the grove of Diana Nemorensis at Lake Nemi, whose priest, the rex Nemorensis, won office by killing his predecessor. Aristodemus of Cumae and the Latins defeated Arruns Porsenna here c. 504 BC.

places.name: Lanuvium
places.summary: Latin town of Juno Sospita, whose cult the Roman consuls shared after 338 BC. Birthplace of Antoninus Pius; a burial club inscription of AD 136 (CIL XIV 2112) preserves a collegium's rules.

places.name: Veii
places.summary: Southern Etruria's largest city, 17 km from Rome, captured by Camillus in 396 BC after a ten-year siege (tradition says by tunnelling under the walls). The conquest doubled Rome's territory. The Portonaccio sanctuary yielded the terracotta Apollo of Veii (c. 510 BC).

places.name: Caere

status.t: civitas sine suffragio (date disputed, 353 or 273 BC)

places.summary: Etruscan city with the Banditaccia necropolis of tumulus tombs. It sheltered the Vestals and sacra during the Gallic sack, and became the model of citizenship without vote: the 'tabulae Caerites' were the census list of half-citizens.

places.name: Tarquinii
places.summary: Etruscan city of the painted tombs (Monterozzi), traditional home of the Tarquin dynasty. Fought Rome 358-351 BC (307 Roman prisoners sacrificed in its forum, Livy 7.15); the Elogia Tarquiniensia record its magistrates.

places.name: Volsinii
places.modern: Orvieto (old city) and Bolsena (new city), Italy
places.foundedNote: Etruscan Velzna on the Orvieto cliff

status.t: destroyed; population moved to Volsinii Novi (Bolsena)

places.summary: Etruscan Velzna, federal sanctuary of the Fanum Voltumnae. After a revolt of its freedmen (or serfs) in 265 BC Rome sacked it in 264, carried off 2,000 statues, and resettled the people at Volsinii Novi on Lake Bolsena.

places.name: Clusium
places.summary: City of Lars Porsenna, who besieged Rome in 508/507 BC. Its appeal against the Senones in 391 BC brought the Gauls into contact with Rome.

places.name: Arretium
places.summary: Etruscan bronze-working city (the Chimera of Arezzo) and, under Augustus, the centre of red-gloss terra sigillata produced in workshops like that of M. Perennius and exported from Britain to India. Maecenas's family came from here.

places.name: Perusia
places.summary: Etruscan city besieged by Octavian in winter 41-40 BC when L. Antonius and Fulvia held it: inscribed sling bullets survive, some obscene. On its fall it burned and Octavian is said to have sacrificed 300 notables at an altar of Divus Iulius (Suet. Aug. 15).

places.name: Falerii

status.t: destroyed; population moved to Falerii Novi

places.summary: Chief city of the Faliscans, Latin-speaking but Etruscan in culture. After its revolt in 241 BC it was destroyed within six days and its people moved to a walled site 5 km west (Falerii Novi).

places.name: Cosa
places.summary: Latin colony on a hill above the Tyrrhenian coast whose excavation by the American Academy (F. E. Brown, 1948-) made it the type-site for mid-Republican colonial planning: polygonal walls, forum, comitium and Capitolium. Its harbour shipped Sestius family amphorae.

places.name: Pyrgi
places.summary: Caere's port and sanctuary of Uni-Astarte, where three gold tablets of c. 500 BC (two Etruscan, one Phoenician) record a dedication by Thefarie Velianas. Dionysius I of Syracuse sacked the temple in 384 BC for 1,000 talents.

places.name: Capua
places.summary: The richest city of Italy in the 4th-3rd centuries BC. Its defection to Hannibal in 216 and recapture in 211 after a siege led to executions of its senate and the confiscation of the ager Campanus. Spartacus broke out of Lentulus Batiatus's gladiatorial school here in 73 BC.

places.name: Neapolis
places.foundedNote: Cumaean foundation c. 470 BC beside Parthenope
places.summary: Greek city that allied with Rome in 326 BC and stayed culturally Greek into late antiquity, with games (Sebasta) founded for Augustus. Belisarius took it in 536 by sending men through an aqueduct; the last western emperor, Romulus, lived nearby at the Castellum Lucullanum.

places.name: Puteoli
places.foundedNote: citizen colony 194 BC on Greek Dicaearchia
places.summary: Italy's chief port before Portus, receiving the Alexandrian grain fleet and eastern goods; its volcanic ash (pulvis puteolanus) made Roman hydraulic concrete. Caligula built a 5 km bridge of boats from here to Baiae; Paul landed here in 61.

places.name: Misenum
places.foundedNote: fleet base established c. 12 BC by Agrippa

status.t: treaty of Misenum between the triumvirs and Sextus Pompey

places.summary: Headquarters of the senior Italian fleet, from which the prefect Pliny the Elder sailed to his death in the eruption of 79. Marines from Misenum formed I Adiutrix in 68, and Tiberius died at Lucullus's villa here in 37.

places.name: Cumae
places.foundedNote: Euboean colony, oldest Greek foundation on the Italian mainland
places.summary: Euboean colony of the mid-8th century BC whose alphabet passed to the Etruscans and Latins. Seat of the Sibyl; Hiero of Syracuse's victory here over the Etruscans in 474 BC broke Etruscan sea power. Ostrogothic treasure was held on its acropolis until 553.

places.name: Pompeii
places.foundedNote: Oscan town; Samnite in the 5th century BC

status.t: besieged by Sulla in the Social War

places.summary: Campanian town of perhaps 10,000-12,000 buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, giving an unmatched picture of urban life: election slogans, graffiti, the Villa of the Mysteries, the riot in the amphitheatre in 59 (Tac. Ann. 14.17). The date of the eruption (24 August or October) is disputed.

places.name: Herculaneum
places.summary: Small seaside town buried under 20 m of pyroclastic flow in 79. The Villa of the Papyri, probably of L. Calpurnius Piso, yielded a carbonised library of Epicurean texts (Philodemus) now being read by X-ray tomography; about 300 skeletons were found in the boathouses.

places.name: Paestum
places.foundedNote: Greek Poseidonia c. 600 BC; Lucanian c. 400; Latin colony 273 BC
places.summary: Sybarite Poseidonia, Lucanian Paistom and the Latin colony of 273 BC, with three Doric temples and the painted Tomb of the Diver (c. 470 BC). It kept the right to mint bronze coins under Tiberius.

places.name: Beneventum
places.summary: Samnite Maleventum, renamed Beneventum after Pyrrhus's defeat nearby in 275 BC. Junction of the Via Appia and Via Traiana, marked by the Arch of Trajan (114). Later the centre of the Lombard duchy of Benevento.

places.name: Aesernia
places.summary: Latin colony in Samnium that held out against the Italian rebels until starved into surrender in 90 BC, and then served as their last capital.

places.name: Venusia
places.summary: Latin colony founded with, says Dionysius, 20,000 settlers to watch the Samnites and Apulians. It took in the survivors of Cannae under Varro in 216 BC. Birthplace of Horace (65 BC).

places.name: Luceria
places.summary: Apulian town that Rome held as a base against the Samnites; its relief was the aim of the march that ended at the Caudine Forks in 321 BC. Latin colony 314 BC.

places.name: Cannae

status.t: site of Hannibal's victory, 2 August 216 BC

places.summary: Apulian hilltop town on the Aufidus (Ofanto) whose grain depot Hannibal seized in 216 BC, drawing the Romans into the battle of 2 August. Whether the fighting was on the right or left bank is still disputed.

places.name: Tarentum

status.t: colonia Neptunia beside the Greek city

places.summary: The richest Greek city of Italy, whose call to Pyrrhus (281 BC) brought the first war between Rome and a Hellenistic king. Taken by Hannibal in 212 except for the citadel, retaken by Fabius in 209. Octavian and Antony renewed their pact here in 37 BC.

places.name: Brundisium
places.summary: Rome's gateway to Greece and the East at the end of the Via Appia. Pompey escaped Caesar's blockade here in March 49 BC; the Treaty of Brundisium (40 BC) divided the empire between Antony and Octavian; Virgil died here in 19 BC.

places.name: Rhegium
places.summary: Chalcidian city on the Straits. Its Campanian garrison seized the town in 280 BC; Rome retook it in 270 and beheaded 300 survivors in the Forum. Endpoint of the Via Popillia.

places.name: Croton
places.summary: Achaean city of Pythagoras and Milo. Hannibal spent his last Italian summer near here and set up a bronze tablet in Punic and Greek recording his campaigns in the temple of Hera Lacinia, which Polybius read (3.33, 3.56).

places.name: Thurii
places.foundedNote: Panhellenic colony 444/443 BC; Latin colony Copia 193 BC

status.t: appeals to Rome against the Lucanians

places.summary: Athenian-led Panhellenic colony near ruined Sybaris (Herodotus and Protagoras were among its settlers). Rome's naval intervention to protect it in 282 BC provoked the war with Tarentum and Pyrrhus.

places.name: Locri Epizephyrii
places.summary: Greek city with the earliest written law code in the Greek West (Zaleucus). In 205-204 BC Scipio's legate Pleminius plundered the temple of Persephone, a scandal that almost cost Scipio his African command (Livy 29.8-22).

places.name: Metapontum
places.summary: Achaean colony famed for its grain (ear of barley on its coins) and its surveyed rural landscape of farm plots. Pythagoras died here; the inhabitants left with Hannibal in 207 BC.

places.name: Heraclea

status.t: treaty with Rome on very favourable terms

places.summary: Site of Pyrrhus's first victory over the Romans (280 BC). The two bronze Tabulae Heracleenses carry a Greek temple-land survey on one face and a Roman law on municipal government (the 'lex Iulia municipalis') on the other.

places.name: Sipontum
places.summary: Apulian port and citizen colony of 194 BC, one of eight maritime colonies founded after the Second Punic War to guard the coasts of southern Italy.

places.name: Bovianum
places.summary: Chief town of the Pentri Samnites, taken by Roman armies in 311 and 305 BC and briefly the rebel capital in the Social War.

places.name: Fregellae
places.summary: Latin colony on the Liris whose foundation in 328 BC triggered the Second Samnite War. It revolted in 125 BC after the failure of proposals to enfranchise the allies, and the praetor L. Opimius razed it; Fabrateria Nova replaced it.

places.name: Minturnae
places.summary: Citizen colony at the Liris mouth on the Via Appia. Gaius Marius hid in its marshes in 88 BC and a Cimbric slave sent to kill him reportedly could not ('I cannot kill Gaius Marius').

places.name: Formiae
places.summary: Coastal town on the Via Appia with villas of the Roman elite. Cicero was murdered by Antony's soldiers near his villa here on 7 December 43 BC.

places.name: Tarracina
places.summary: Volscian Anxur on the Via Appia, citizen colony 329 BC, crowned by the temple of Jupiter Anxur. Trajan's engineers cut the Pisco Montano 36 m vertically to carry the road along the coast, with the depth marked in Roman feet.

places.name: Norba
places.summary: Latin colony on the edge of the Lepini with polygonal walls 2.5 km long. Marian sympathisers held it against Sulla in 82 BC and killed each other rather than surrender; it was never rebuilt.

places.name: Alba Fucens
places.summary: Latin colony in Aequian territory used as a high-security prison for royal captives: Syphax of Numidia, Perseus of Macedon and the Arvernian king Bituitus died here.

places.name: Corfinium
places.summary: Paelignian town renamed Italia in 90 BC as capital of the Italian allies' state, with its own senate of 500 and coinage showing the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf. In February 49 BC L. Domitius Ahenobarbus surrendered it to Caesar, who released him: the first act of clementia.

places.name: Asculum

status.t: massacre of Romans opens the Social War

places.summary: Picene town where the murder of the praetor Q. Servilius and all Romans in late 91 BC began the Social War. Pompeius Strabo took it in 89 after a siege documented by inscribed sling bullets. (Pyrrhus's battle of Asculum, 279 BC, was at Ausculum in Apulia.)

places.name: Ancona
places.summary: Syracusan Greek port, the 'elbow' (ankon) of the Adriatic. Trajan rebuilt the harbour for his Dacian wars, commemorated by his arch of 115 on the mole.

places.name: Ariminum
places.summary: Latin colony at the junction of the Via Flaminia, Via Aemilia and Via Popillia, the gateway to Cisalpine Gaul. Caesar's first stop after the Rubicon (January 49 BC). The Arch of Augustus (27 BC) and the bridge of Tiberius (AD 21) still stand; the council of Ariminum (359) produced an Arian-leaning creed.

places.name: Sena Gallica
places.foundedNote: citizen colony c. 283 BC on Senonian land
places.summary: Citizen colony planted on the land of the Senones after their defeat (284/283 BC). Near it on the Metaurus Hasdrubal Barca was destroyed in 207 BC; Narses defeated the Gothic fleet off it in 551.

places.name: Fanum Fortunae
places.foundedNote: town at the Via Flaminia's Adriatic outlet; Augustan colony
places.summary: Town where the Via Flaminia reaches the Adriatic, occupied by Caesar in 49 BC. Vitruvius designed and built its basilica (De arch. 5.1.6). The Arch of Augustus (AD 9) survives.

places.name: Spoletium
places.summary: Umbrian Latin colony that repulsed Hannibal's assault after Trasimene in 217 BC. Later seat of the Lombard duchy of Spoleto.

places.name: Narnia
places.foundedNote: Latin colony 299 BC on Umbrian Nequinum
places.summary: Latin colony on the Nar guarding the Via Flaminia, whose Bridge of Augustus (c. 27 BC) is one of the largest Roman bridges. Birthplace of the emperor Nerva (30).

places.name: Reate
places.summary: Sabine town on the Via Salaria, the umbilicus of Italy in Varro's reckoning. Vespasian was born at Falacrina nearby (AD 9); Varro the scholar was a native.

places.name: Bononia
places.foundedNote: Etruscan Felsina, Boian city; Latin colony 189 BC
places.summary: Etruscan Felsina, then Boian; Latin colony in 189 BC on the Via Aemilia. On an island in a river near here Antony, Octavian and Lepidus agreed the Second Triumvirate in October 43 BC.

places.name: Mutina
places.summary: Citizen colony on the Via Aemilia besieged by Antony in winter 44-43 BC while held by Decimus Brutus. Both consuls, Hirtius and Pansa, died in the relieving battles of April 43, leaving Octavian in command.

places.name: Parma
places.summary: Citizen colony on the Via Aemilia founded with Mutina in 183 BC, known for its wool. In 553 Narses's general Fulcaris was killed by the Franks near here.

places.name: Placentia
places.summary: Latin colony founded with Cremona in 218 BC on the Po, months before Hannibal arrived; it survived the war. End of the Via Aemilia. Caesar faced the mutiny of the IX here in 49 BC; Avitus was deposed and made bishop here in 456.

places.name: Cremona
places.summary: Latin colony on the north bank of the Po. After the second battle of Bedriacum (October 69) the Flavian troops sacked and burned it for four days (Tac. Hist. 3.32-34).

places.name: Bedriacum
places.summary: Village on the Via Postumia that named the two battles of 69: Vitellius's victory over Otho (14 April) and the Flavian victory over Vitellius (24-25 October).

places.name: Mediolanum
places.summary: Insubrian city that became the western imperial capital under Maximian (286) and remained so until 402. Constantine and Licinius agreed the religious settlement here in 313; Ambrose, bishop 374-397, defied Valentinian II and Theodosius. Sacked by the Goths in 539 with terrible loss of life.

places.name: Comum
places.summary: Town at the south of Lake Como refounded by Caesar under the lex Vatinia; the flogging of a Comum decurion by Marcellus in 51 BC was a calculated insult to Caesar. Birthplace of both Plinys.

places.name: Verona
places.summary: Town on the Adige that controlled the route to the Brenner. Its amphitheatre is the third largest surviving. Constantine besieged it in 312; Stilicho defeated Alaric near it in 402/403; Theodoric favoured it (the 'Bern' of German legend).

places.name: Aquileia
places.summary: Latin colony at the head of the Adriatic, base for the Alpine and Danubian wars and trade in amber. Maximinus Thrax was murdered by his own troops besieging it in 238. Attila destroyed it in 452; refugees fled to the lagoons.

places.name: Patavium
places.summary: Venetic city famed for its wealth: Strabo (5.1.7) says its census had 500 equites, as many as any city but Rome. Livy's birthplace; Asinius Pollio mocked his Patavinitas.

places.name: Ravenna
places.summary: Lagoon town Honorius chose as capital in 402 for its defensibility. Capital of Odoacer and Theodoric (who took it after a three-year siege in 493) and of Byzantine Italy. Its mosaics (Galla Placidia, San Vitale with Justinian and Theodora, 547) are the finest of late antiquity.

places.name: Classis
places.summary: Augustan fleet harbour of Ravenna for 250 ships (Jordanes). The basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe was dedicated in 549; Liutprand's Lombards destroyed the port c. 725.

places.name: Genua

status.t: destroyed by Mago, rebuilt by Rome

places.summary: Ligurian port allied to Rome, destroyed by Mago Barca in 205 BC and rebuilt. The Sententia Minuciorum (117 BC) on a bronze tablet settles its boundary dispute with the Langenses Veiturii.

places.name: Luna
places.summary: Citizen colony at the Magra mouth that shipped Carrara (Luna) marble to Rome from Caesar's time on; the Pantheon portico and Trajan's column used it.

places.name: Pisae
places.summary: Etruscan port at the Arno mouth, Rome's base against the Ligurians. The Cenotaphia Pisana record the town's grief for Augustus's grandsons Lucius (d. 2) and Gaius (d. 4).

places.name: Florentia
places.foundedNote: colony c. 59 BC (Caesar) or triumviral 41 BC
places.summary: Colony on the Arno laid out as a castrum. Stilicho destroyed Radagaisus's army at Faesulae nearby in 406.

places.name: Augusta Taurinorum
places.summary: Augustan colony on the Taurini lands at the foot of the western Alpine passes; its Porta Palatina survives. Constantine won a cavalry battle here in 312.

places.name: Augusta Praetoria Salassorum
places.summary: Colony founded by Varro Murena after he crushed the Salassi in 25 BC, selling 36,000 into slavery. It controlled both St Bernard passes; its gates and theatre survive.

places.name: Tergeste
places.summary: Colony at the head of the Adriatic whose walls were built by Octavian in 33 BC (CIL V 525).

places.name: Pola
places.foundedNote: Colonia Pietas Iulia Pola, Caesarian or triumviral
places.summary: Istrian colony whose amphitheatre (23,000 seats) is among the best preserved. Constantine had his son Crispus executed here in 326.

places.name: Brixia
places.summary: Cenomanian town with a Flavian Capitolium (73). The bronze Victory of Brescia was found hidden in the temple.

places.name: Ticinum
places.summary: Town on the Ticinus near which Hannibal's cavalry beat P. Scipio in late 218 BC. Imperial mint from 274; Odoacer killed Orestes here in 476. Capital of the Lombard kingdom from 572.

places.name: Altinum
places.summary: Lagoon port and start of the Via Claudia Augusta. Its people moved to Torcello and the islands of the future Venice in the 5th-7th centuries.

places.name: Castra Albana
places.foundedNote: fortress of II Parthica built c. 202
places.summary: Severan fortress for II Parthica on Domitian's Alban estate, 20 km from Rome on the Via Appia: the first legionary base in Italy.

places.name: Baiae
places.summary: Volcanic spa of the Roman elite, notorious for luxury (Seneca, Ep. 51). Agrippina the Younger was murdered at her villa near here in 59 after the collapsing-boat plot failed; Hadrian died here in 138. Much of it now lies underwater from bradyseism.

places.name: Capreae
places.summary: Island exchanged by Augustus with Naples for Ischia. Tiberius ruled the empire from the Villa Jovis here from 27 to 37.

places.name: Caudium
places.summary: Samnite town near the pass of the Caudine Forks, where in 321 BC both consular armies surrendered to Gavius Pontius and passed under the yoke.

places.name: Syracusae

status.t: captured by Marcellus; seat of the governor of Sicilia

places.summary: Largest Greek city of the West. After Hiero II's death it joined Carthage; Marcellus took it in 212 BC after a two-year siege resisted by Archimedes' machines, and Archimedes was killed. Capital of Sicilia; Verres's plunder of its art drew Cicero's prosecution (70 BC).

places.name: Agrigentum
places.summary: Akragas of the Valley of the Temples. Rome's capture of the Carthaginian base here in 262 BC was the first great land success of the First Punic War.

places.name: Panormus
places.summary: Punic city taken by Rome in 254 BC. Under its walls in 250 BC L. Caecilius Metellus routed Hasdrubal and captured his elephants, displayed in Rome's circus; the elephant became a Metellan coin type.

places.name: Lilybaeum
places.foundedNote: founded after the destruction of Motya (397 BC)
places.summary: Carthaginian fortress at Sicily's western tip besieged by Rome from 250 to 241 BC. Cicero served as quaestor here in 75 BC; Scipio sailed from it to Africa in 204.

places.name: Drepana
places.summary: Carthaginian naval base off which P. Claudius Pulcher lost 93 ships in 249 BC after throwing the sacred chickens overboard ('let them drink, since they won't eat').

places.name: Eryx
places.summary: Mountain sanctuary of Venus Erycina, the Phoenician Astarte. Hamilcar Barca held the slopes from 244 to 241 BC; the goddess received a temple on the Capitol in 215.

places.name: Segesta

status.t: ally of Rome, civitas libera et immunis

places.summary: Elymian city that went over to Rome in 263 BC claiming common Trojan descent, and was rewarded with freedom from tribute. Its unfinished Doric temple stands intact.

places.name: Messana
places.summary: Greek Zancle, seized c. 288 BC by Campanian mercenaries, the Mamertines. Their appeal to Rome in 264 BC against Hiero and Carthage started the First Punic War.

places.name: Tauromenium
places.foundedNote: founded 358 BC by refugees from Naxos
places.summary: Greek city with a theatre facing Etna. It took Sextus Pompey's side; Octavian expelled its people and planted a colony in 21 BC.

places.name: Catana
places.summary: Chalcidian city on the slopes of Etna, Augustan colony after the war with Sextus Pompey. Agatha was martyred here under Decius (251).

places.name: Henna

status.t: centre of the First Slave War

places.summary: Inland fortress and cult site of Demeter and Kore. In 135 BC the Syrian slave Eunus, who breathed fire, proclaimed himself King Antiochus here; the Romans took it only in 132.

places.name: Carales

status.t: Roman from the seizure of Sardinia

places.summary: Phoenician port, capital of Sardinia et Corsica. Its Roman amphitheatre is cut into the rock. Vandal possession from c. 456 to 533.

places.name: Nora
places.summary: Phoenician town whose Nora Stone (9th-8th century BC) is one of the earliest Phoenician inscriptions in the West and first to name Sardinia (ŠRDN).

places.name: Tharros
places.summary: Phoenician-Punic port on the Sinis peninsula, rich in tophet burials and Punic gold; its Roman town survived into the 11th century.

places.name: Aleria
places.summary: Phocaean Alalia, whose sea battle with the Etruscans and Carthaginians c. 540 BC split the western sea into spheres. L. Cornelius Scipio took it in 259 BC (his epitaph: 'hec cepit Corsica Aleriaque urbe').

places.name: Gades
places.summary: Phoenician Gadir on its island, with the temple of Melqart-Hercules where Caesar reportedly wept before Alexander's statue. It went over to Rome in 206 BC; by Augustus it had 500 equites (Strabo 3.5.3). Home of the Balbi, the first foreign-born consul (40 BC).

places.name: Carthago Nova
places.foundedNote: founded c. 228/227 BC by Hasdrubal the Fair as Qart Hadasht
places.summary: Barcid capital stormed by Scipio in 209 BC across a lagoon he knew would ebb. Its silver mines employed 40,000 workers yielding 25,000 drachmae a day (Polybius in Strabo 3.2.10). Capital of Byzantine Spania (552-c.625).

places.name: Saguntum
places.summary: Iberian city allied with Rome whose eight-month siege and capture by Hannibal (219 BC) was the casus belli of the Second Punic War, though the legality under the Ebro treaty was argued then and since.

places.name: Emporiae
places.summary: Greek trading town where Cn. Scipio landed in 218 BC and Cato the Elder began his Spanish campaign in 195. A Roman town grew beside the Greek one, merged under Augustus.

places.name: Tarraco
places.foundedNote: Scipionic base 218 BC on Iberian Kesse
places.summary: Base of the Scipios from 218 BC and capital of the largest Spanish province. Augustus spent the winter of 26-25 BC here ill during the Cantabrian war; the provincial temple of Augustus (AD 15) was a model for imperial cult in the West. Fructuosus was burned here in 259.

places.name: Italica
places.foundedNote: founded 206 BC by Scipio for wounded soldiers (Appian, Iber. 38)
places.summary: The first Roman settlement in Spain, founded by Scipio after Ilipa. Home of the Ulpii and Aelii: Trajan was born here and Hadrian's family came from it. Hadrian built a vast new quarter (nova urbs) and a 25,000-seat amphitheatre.

places.name: Corduba
places.foundedNote: founded by M. Claudius Marcellus, 169 or 152 BC
places.summary: Capital of Baetica. Caesar's troops killed 22,000 here after Munda (45 BC). Birthplace of the two Senecas and Lucan; its bishop Ossius advised Constantine and presided at Nicaea in 325.

places.name: Hispalis
places.summary: Port on the Baetis reachable by seagoing ships, refounded by Caesar as Colonia Iulia Romula. Shipped Baetican olive oil to Rome, where its amphorae (Dressel 20) built the Monte Testaccio. Gunderic's Vandals took it in 428.

places.name: Emerita Augusta
places.foundedNote: founded 25 BC by P. Carisius for veterans of V Alaudae and X Gemina
places.summary: Veteran colony at a Guadiana crossing, with one of the longest Roman bridges (c. 790 m), the theatre given by Agrippa (16-15 BC), and the Los Milagros aqueduct. Capital of Lusitania and of the late diocese of the Spains.

places.name: Toletum
places.summary: Carpetanian stronghold taken in 193 BC. It became the Visigothic capital under Athanagild and Leovigild; at the Third Council of Toledo (589) King Reccared renounced Arianism.

places.name: Numantia
places.summary: Celtiberian city of perhaps 8,000 that defeated Roman armies for twenty years (153-133 BC); the capitulation of Mancinus in 137 was repudiated by the Senate. Scipio Aemilianus enclosed it with a 9 km circumvallation and seven camps and starved it out; Adolf Schulten excavated the camps (1905-12).

places.name: Caesaraugusta
places.foundedNote: colony c. 14 BC on Iberian Salduie
places.summary: Colony for veterans of IV Macedonica, VI Victrix and X Gemina, on the Ebro. The Bronze of Contrebia (87 BC) and the Turma Salluitana (89 BC, Iberian cavalry from Salduie given citizenship by Pompeius Strabo) come from its area.

places.name: Osca
places.summary: Sertorius's capital, where he founded a school to educate the sons of Spanish nobles in Greek and Latin (Plut. Sert. 14). He was assassinated at a banquet here by Perperna in 73/72 BC.

places.name: Ilerda
places.summary: Town on the Segre where Caesar outmanoeuvred Pompey's legates Afranius and Petreius in 49 BC and forced their surrender without a pitched battle by cutting their water.

places.name: Valentia
places.foundedNote: founded 138 BC by D. Junius Brutus Callaicus
places.summary: Founded in 138 BC by D. Junius Brutus for soldiers who had fought under (or against) Viriathus (Livy Per. 55). Pompey destroyed it in 75 BC after defeating Sertorius's men; excavations found their mutilated skeletons.

places.name: Carteia
places.summary: First Latin colony outside Italy, founded in 171 BC for 4,000 sons of Roman soldiers and Spanish women (Livy 43.3). Gnaeus Pompeius the Younger fled here after Munda.

places.name: Baelo Claudia
places.summary: Fishing town on the Strait of Gibraltar with garum salting vats, forum and Capitolium, made a municipium by Claudius when Mauretania was annexed.

places.name: Malaca
places.summary: Phoenician port whose bronze Lex Flavia Malacitana (81-84) preserves the charter of a Latin municipium, with election rules. Byzantine from 552.

places.name: Urso
places.summary: Pompeian stronghold after Munda, refounded by Caesar's posthumous law as Colonia Genetiva Iulia for urban plebs. Its bronze charter, the Lex Ursonensis, is the fullest colonial charter surviving.

places.name: Legio
places.foundedNote: fortress of VII Gemina from 74; earlier camp of VI Victrix
places.summary: Fortress whose name became León. Base of VI Victrix and then for four centuries of VII Gemina, which policed Asturia and the gold mines.

places.name: Asturica Augusta
places.foundedNote: Augustan foundation c. 14 BC on a military site
places.summary: Capital of the Asturian conventus and seat of the procurator of the gold mines, who drew on mines such as Las Médulas.

places.name: Lucus Augusti
places.summary: Conventus capital of Gallaecia, whose late-Roman walls (c. 263-276, 2 km with 85 towers) are the only complete Roman circuit surviving in the West.

places.name: Bracara Augusta
places.summary: Capital of Gallaecia from Diocletian's reforms and of the Suevic kingdom (411-585). Martin of Braga converted the Suevi to Catholicism in the 550s-560s.

places.name: Olisipo
places.summary: Atlantic port at the Tagus mouth, municipium of Roman citizens under Augustus. Lisbon's theatre was dedicated to Nero in 57.

places.name: Conimbriga
places.summary: Lusitanian town with superb mosaics (House of the Fountains). Its 4th-century wall cut the town in half; the Suevi sacked it in 465 and 468 (Hydatius).

places.name: Clunia
places.summary: Conventus capital in the Meseta where Galba learned of Nero's death in June 68; he raised it to a colony named Sulpicia after his own gens.

places.name: Pompaelo
places.foundedNote: founded by Pompey in winter 75/74 BC
places.summary: Town of the Vascones named after Pompey, who wintered here in 75/74 BC during the Sertorian war.

places.name: Barcino
places.foundedNote: Colonia Iulia Augusta Faventia Paterna Barcino, c. 15-10 BC
places.summary: Small Augustan colony with strong late-Roman walls. The Gothic king Athaulf, husband of Galla Placidia, was murdered in its palace in 415.

places.name: Munda
places.summary: Town near which Caesar defeated Gnaeus and Sextus Pompeius on 17 March 45 BC, saying he had often fought for victory but here for his life (Plut. Caes. 56). The site is disputed (Llanos de Vanda near Osuna, Montilla, La Lantejuela).

places.name: Castulo
places.summary: Oretanian city controlling the silver-lead mines of the Sierra Morena. Hannibal's wife Imilce was from here; P. Scipio (father) was killed near it in 211 BC.

places.name: Mines of Rio Tinto
places.summary: Copper and silver mines of the Iberian pyrite belt, worked from the Bronze Age. Roman galleries were drained by chains of wooden water-wheels, and some 16 million tonnes of Roman-era slag survive.

places.name: Las Médulas
places.summary: The largest Roman gold mine, worked by ruina montium: galleries flooded from aqueducts brought down whole hillsides (Pliny NH 33.70-78). Pliny says Asturia, Gallaecia and Lusitania yielded 20,000 pounds of gold a year.

places.name: Sisapo
places.summary: Source of cinnabar (minium) for vermilion, a state monopoly leased to a company; Pliny says 10,000 pounds a year were sent sealed to Rome to be refined (NH 33.118).

places.name: Segovia
places.summary: Celtiberian town whose aqueduct bridge (late 1st or early 2nd century, 28 m high, of granite without mortar) is the best preserved in the Roman world.

places.name: Ilipa
places.summary: Town on the Baetis near which Scipio defeated Hasdrubal Gisco and Mago in 206 BC by reversing his usual deployment, ending Carthaginian power in Spain.

places.name: Massalia
places.summary: Phocaean city and Rome's oldest ally in the West, whose calls for help brought Rome into Transalpine Gaul (125-121 BC). It sided with Pompey, endured Caesar's siege in 49 BC (Trebonius's siege mound, D. Brutus's fleet) and lost most of its territory.

places.name: Narbo Martius
places.summary: Founded in 118 BC on the Via Domitia, Rome's first citizen colony overseas, championed by the orator L. Licinius Crassus. It gave the province its name. Theodoric II received it from the usurper Libius Severus's regime in 462.

places.name: Arelate
places.foundedNote: Colonia Iulia Paterna Arelatensium Sextanorum, 46 BC

status.t: seat of the praetorian prefect of Gaul (c. 395-407)

places.summary: Caesar rewarded it for building twelve ships against Massalia. Constantine resided here; the council of 314 met to judge the Donatists. Seat of the Gallic prefecture from c. 395-407 and of the Council of the Seven Provinces (418).

places.name: Nemausus
places.summary: Colony whose coins show a crocodile chained to a palm, celebrating Egyptian veterans after Actium. The Maison Carrée (c. 2 BC-AD 4/5, for Gaius and Lucius Caesar) and the Pont du Gard aqueduct (mid-1st century) survive. Family home of Antoninus Pius.

places.name: Forum Iulii
places.summary: Colony of veterans of VIII; the ships captured at Actium were based here (Tac. Ann. 4.5). Birthplace of Agricola (40).

places.name: Aquae Sextiae
places.foundedNote: fort founded 122 BC by C. Sextius Calvinus
places.summary: The first Roman settlement in Gaul, a garrison post founded after the defeat of the Salluvii. Marius annihilated the Teutones and Ambrones nearby in 102 BC.

places.name: Vienna
places.summary: Chief town of the Allobroges on the Rhône with the temple of Augustus and Livia. Valentinian II died (hanged) here in 392 while under Arbogast's control.

places.name: Lugdunum
places.foundedNote: founded 43 BC by L. Munatius Plancus (Copia Felix Munatia)

status.t: capital of Lugdunensis; hub of Agrippa's roads

places.summary: Capital of the Three Gauls at the Rhône-Saône confluence, with the federal Altar of Rome and Augustus (12 BC) and an imperial mint. Claudius was born here (10 BC); his speech on admitting Gauls to the Senate survives on the Lyon tablet. Martyrs of 177 (Blandina); Severus defeated Albinus here in 197.

places.name: Tolosa
places.summary: Town of the Volcae Tectosages whose temple treasure, the 'gold of Tolosa', was seized by Q. Servilius Caepio in 106 BC and vanished; Caepio's disaster at Arausio was blamed on it. Capital of the Visigothic kingdom 418-507.

places.name: Burdigala
places.summary: Atlantic tin and wine port, later capital of Aquitania. Ausonius taught rhetoric here before becoming tutor to Gratian; the Bordeaux pilgrim set out from here to Jerusalem in 333.

places.name: Lutetia Parisiorum
places.summary: Town of the Parisii on the Île de la Cité. Julian wintered here and was proclaimed Augustus by his troops in 360; Clovis made it his capital in 508.

places.name: Augustodunum
places.foundedNote: founded c. 15 BC to replace Bibracte
places.summary: New capital of the Aedui with a 6 km wall and gates that still stand. Its schools (scholae Maenianae) trained Gallic elites; Sacrovir's rebels seized the students here in 21. Restored after Tetricus's siege by Constantius I (speech of Eumenius, 298).

places.name: Bibracte
places.summary: Hill-town of the Aedui on Mont Beuvray, 135 ha within its walls. Caesar fought the Helvetii near it (58 BC); in 52 BC the Gallic council confirmed Vercingetorix as supreme commander here, and Caesar wintered here writing up the war.

places.name: Alesia
places.summary: Hill fortress on Mont Auxois where Caesar besieged Vercingetorix in 52 BC inside 15 km of contravallation and 21 km of circumvallation against a relief army Caesar puts at 250,000. Napoleon III's excavations (1861-65) and Franco-German work (1991-97) confirmed the lines.

places.name: Gergovia
places.summary: Arvernian stronghold where Caesar's assault failed in 52 BC with the loss of 46 centurions and 700 men, his only serious defeat in Gaul.

places.name: Avaricum
places.summary: Biturigan town that the Gauls refused to burn in 52 BC; Caesar took it after a 25-day siege with a terrace 330 feet wide and says only 800 of 40,000 escaped (BG 7.28).

places.name: Cenabum

status.t: massacre of Roman traders; sacked by Caesar

places.summary: Carnutian town on the Loire where the massacre of Roman merchants in January 52 BC signalled the great revolt. Renamed Aurelianis; its relief from Attila in 451 under bishop Anianus preceded the Catalaunian Plains.

places.name: Durocortorum
places.summary: Capital of the Remi, Caesar's loyal allies, and of Gallia Belgica; the Porte de Mars is a 3rd-century triumphal arch. Bishop Remigius baptised Clovis here (496 or 508).

places.name: Samarobriva
places.summary: Ambianian town on the Somme where Caesar held a council of Gaul in 54 BC. Here the soldier Martin cut his cloak for a beggar (c. 337).

places.name: Gesoriacum
places.foundedNote: Morinian port; Bononia from the 3rd century
places.summary: Main Channel port and headquarters of the British fleet, where Caligula built a lighthouse (the Tour d'Odre) and the Claudian invasion embarked. Carausius held it until Constantius I blockaded and took it in 293.

places.name: Divodurum
places.summary: Mediomatrican town where Vitellius's troops massacred 4,000 inhabitants in a panic in 69 (Tac. Hist. 1.63). Sacked by Attila on Easter eve 451.

places.name: Augusta Treverorum
places.foundedNote: founded c. 16 BC (bridge timbers dated 18/17 BC)

status.t: imperial residence and prefecture of Gaul

places.summary: Treveran capital that became the residence of the Gallic emperors and then of Constantius I, Constantine, Valentinian I and Gratian. The Porta Nigra (c. 170), the Aula Palatina, the imperial baths and the cathedral core survive; Salvian says it was sacked four times in the early 5th century.

places.name: Arausio
places.foundedNote: veteran colony of II Gallica 35 BC
places.summary: Near here on 6 October 105 BC the Cimbri and Teutones destroyed the armies of Caepio and Mallius Maximus, Rome's worst defeat since Cannae (Livy Per. 67: 80,000 soldiers). The colony has the best preserved Roman theatre stage-wall and an arch, and its cadaster inscriptions map the centuriated land.

places.name: Vesontio
places.summary: Sequanian oppidum in a loop of the Doubs, seized by Caesar in 58 BC before facing Ariovistus. Verginius Rufus's legions destroyed Vindex's Gallic army near it in 68.

places.name: Colonia Iulia Equestris
places.foundedNote: founded c. 45 BC by Caesar for cavalry veterans
places.summary: Caesarian colony on Lake Geneva, settled with veteran cavalrymen to watch the Helvetii after 58 BC.

places.name: Augusta Raurica
places.foundedNote: founded 44 BC by Munatius Plancus; refounded c. 15 BC
places.summary: Rhine colony with the best preserved theatre north of the Alps. The Kaiseraugst treasure (c. 350, 257 silver objects) was buried in the late fort during the Magnentian war.

places.name: Aventicum

status.t: Colonia Pia Flavia Constans Emerita Helvetiorum Foederata

places.summary: Helvetian capital where Vespasian's father ran a banking business; Vespasian made it a colony. A gold bust of Marcus Aurelius was found in its sanctuary drain.

places.name: Mediolanum Santonum
places.summary: Capital of the Santones and first capital of Aquitania, with the Arch of Germanicus (AD 18/19) on the bridge of the Agrippan road from Lugdunum.

places.name: Augustonemetum
places.summary: New Augustan capital of the Arverni. Its bishop Sidonius Apollinaris led the resistance to Euric until the empire ceded it in 475.

places.name: Caesarodunum
places.summary: Capital of the Turones and see of Martin (bishop 371-397), whose shrine made Tours the chief pilgrimage site of Gaul. Gregory of Tours wrote here.

places.name: Lemonum
places.summary: Capital of the Pictones. Hilary was bishop (c. 350-367); Clovis defeated and killed Alaric II at Vouillé near it in 507.
